name: Private Eye Cyclops crossword No 511
preamble: Running clockwise around the shaded squares, starting top left, is an extract from a Diary ‘as told to Craig Brown’. There are minor changes and a hyphen, a dash and two full stops are lacking. The name of the diary’s ‘author’ is the answer to a definition-less clue. Letters of the quote not intersecting with normal clue answers are: AAAAAA C EEEE F G HHH II L MMM NNN OOOOOO PPP RRRRRRR SSSS TT U WWWW

solutions.check: 64 entries verified against the grid image (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping); unclued letters checked against the preamble's list

clue.text: Company suit goes off ‘bang‘

indicators.note: something that goes off has spoiled or exploded, so its letters come out in a new order

blocks.note: CO is the standard abbreviation for company
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A firm's legal action collapses with a loud noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suit' reads as a lawsuit going off with a bang, but it is just four letters to shuffle; the quoted 'bang' is the slang definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Bang is crude slang for an act of sexual intercourse, and coitus is the formal Latin term for the same act.

clue.text: Way to break Sun-backed political body

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it, so one piece sits within another
backed means sent backwards, so the letters run right to left

blocks.note: RD is the abbreviation for road, a way
Sol is the Latin name for the sun

explanation.surface: A road protest disrupts a party that the Sun newspaper has endorsed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sun-backed' looks like the tabloid's endorsement, but it is a reversal instruction. Sol is Latin for the sun, a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: The House of Lords is the upper chamber of the UK Parliament, so it is a legislative assembly, commonly shortened to the Lords.

clue.text: Royal getting end away: “Fabulous in the middle!” “Reverse”

indicators.note: getting an end away means sending its final letter off, so the tail is dropped
only the central part of the word is wanted, the letters at its very centre

blocks.note: Princess Anne, the royal, with her last letter dropped
the two central letters of the eight-letter word

explanation.surface: Gossip about a royal having sex, with excited cries of delight and a call to change position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting end away' is British slang for having sex, but here it lops the last letter off ANNE, Princess Royal.
explanation.definitionFit: To annul a law or marriage is to cancel it and declare it void, which is to reverse or undo it.

clue.text: Drinks provider in the groin area holds large one

indicators.note: whatever holds something keeps it inside, so one part wraps around another

blocks.note: pubic means relating to the groin region
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
an is the indefinite article, meaning one

explanation.surface: A barman keeping a big one in his trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'large one' sounds like a large drink, but it splits into L, placed inside the groin word, and AN tacked on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A publican runs a pub, the British name for a bar, so he is the person who serves beer and spirits to customers.

clue.text: Who gets satisfaction from practising “do unto others as you would have done to you”?

definitions.text: Who gets satisfaction from practising “do unto others as you would have done to you”?

blocks.clueFragment: Who gets satisfaction from practising “do unto others as you would have done to you”?
blocks.note: surface reading: a devout follower of the Golden Rule, kind to others as he wishes others were kind to him

blocks.clueFragment: do unto others as you would have done to you
blocks.note: setter's reading: someone who enjoys both inflicting pain and having pain inflicted, taking 'do' as hurt

explanation.walkthrough: The Golden Rule is a moral teaching about kindness; read with 'do' as meaning cause pain, it describes a person who enjoys both giving and receiving it.
explanation.definitionFit: The word combines sadist and masochist, a person deriving pleasure from inflicting suffering on partners as well as receiving it.

clue.text: TV salary in an immoderate land of bloodsuckers?

indicators.note: something immoderate is out of control and unrestrained, so these letters run wild into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, twelve letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A dig at bloated television pay, as if broadcasters were leeching off the public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In an' looks like linking words, but they belong to the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Transylvania, a region of Romania, is the home of Count Dracula in Bram Stoker's novel, so it is the legendary country of vampires.

clue.text: America unlikely to be source of unwitting leak?

definitions.text: unlikely to be source of unwitting leak

blocks.note: first meaning: one of the great landmasses of the world

blocks.clueFragment: unlikely to be source of unwitting leak
blocks.note: second meaning: in control of bladder and bowels

explanation.walkthrough: The 'unwitting leak' reads as a security slip about the USA, but it is bodily: the opposite of incontinent.
explanation.definitionFit: North and South America are each a large landmass, and the adjective describes someone with full control over urination.

clue.text: Say Mo’s worried about perverse shagging and self-love

indicators.note: worried things are agitated and disturbed, so these letters get churned into a fresh order
perverse means turned the wrong way, so the letters face the opposite direction
about means around, so one set of letters goes round another

blocks.note: e.g., for example, is a way of saying 'say'
taken as written, to be rearranged
it is a coy word for sex

explanation.surface: Mo frets about kinky sex and masturbation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Self-love' tempts as a sexual reference, matching the surface, but it is the definition in its other sense, vanity. IT for sex is a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Egotism is an excessive sense of one's own importance, a conceited preoccupation with oneself, which is vanity or self-regard.

clue.text: Tense love bites forming clots

blocks.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense
hickies are love bites, mostly an American term

explanation.surface: Anxious love bites turning into blood clots on the neck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clots' looks medical, matching love bites, but in British slang a clot is a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Clot and thicky are both informal British insults for a stupid person, so the plurals are synonyms.

clue.text: Well outside the harbour, lad, so now you can kill the wildlife?

definitions.text: now you can kill the wildlife?

blocks.note: the open sea is the water far from the shore and any port
a son is a lad, a boy

explanation.surface: A father tells his boy that, now they are far from port, he may start hunting the sea creatures.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a phrase standing for the period itself, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Open season is the legally permitted period for hunting particular game, when shooting animals is allowed.

clue.text: Catty thing not now keeping you texted

indicators.note: keeping something means holding on to it inside, so one piece is enclosed

blocks.note: once means at some time in the past, not now
U is text-message shorthand for you

explanation.surface: A spiteful remark about not messaging someone back right now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catty' sounds spiteful but just means feline here: an ounce is another name for the snow leopard.
explanation.definitionFit: The ounce, or snow leopard, is a big wild cat of central Asia, so it is literally a cat-like creature.

clue.text: “Margaret must go/depart!”

blocks.note: Peg is a pet form of Margaret
'out!' is the cry demanding that someone must go

explanation.surface: A protest chant demanding that Margaret Thatcher leave office.
explanation.walkthrough: The slash splits the clue: the protest slogan before it is wordplay, and 'depart' after it is the definition, in the sense of die.
explanation.definitionFit: To peg out is informal British slang for dying, and depart is a euphemism for passing away.

clue.text: see 53dn.
Ex-party leader, one demonstrated to welcome Miliband’s extreme right

indicators.note: the extreme right of a word is its far end, the very last letter
to welcome a guest is to take them in, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: a means one
shown means demonstrated
the final letter of the Labour leader's surname

explanation.surface: A former party leader joins a demonstration welcoming Ed Miliband's swing to the right.
explanation.walkthrough: Paddy Ashdown led the Liberal Democrats, and Ed Miliband led Labour when this appeared; 'extreme right' sounds political but is the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Paddy Ashdown led the Liberal Democrats from 1988 to 1999, so he is a former head of a British political party.

clue.text: Blair con, involved with conservative, initially unscrupulous bunch of lawyers

indicators.note: involved means tangled and complicated, so the letters are twisted together into a new order
initially points to the first letter of the following word

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
C is the abbreviation for Conservative
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A dig at Tony Blair as a con man in league with Tories and shady lawyers.
explanation.walkthrough: Cherie Blair is a barrister, which gives the surface its edge; 'Blair con' are plain letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bar Council is the professional body representing barristers in England and Wales, so it is an organised group of lawyers.

clue.text: Bird, slapper taking drugs

indicators.note: taking something in means absorbing it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a beater is someone who slaps or hits
E is ecstasy, so two of them are drugs

explanation.surface: A girl described in crude British slang as promiscuous and doing drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a slapper is a promiscuous woman and a bird is a young woman, so the surface is all about one woman; slapper is really one who slaps. E for ecstasy is a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: The bee-eater is a brightly coloured bird that catches bees and other flying insects, so it is a species of bird.

clue.text: Branson’s thing is like squeezing Cointreau cocktail?

indicators.note: a cocktail is a mixture, so these letters are shaken into a new order
squeezing something means pressing it within, so one part holds another

blocks.note: as means like
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Richard Branson's favourite tipple is a Cointreau cocktail.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Branson founded Virgin Atlantic and Virgin Galactic and made record balloon flights, so flight is his thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Aeronautics is the science and practice of flight, Branson's passion through his airline, spaceflight company and ballooning exploits.

clue.text: Fishy group pissing off – “attending lessons”

blocks.note: a school is a group of fish
pissing off is crude slang for going away

explanation.surface: A suspicious bunch of pupils bunking off class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fishy' suggests suspicious, but it means made of fish: a shoal is also called a school.
explanation.definitionFit: Schoolgoing describes a child who regularly goes to school, so someone at school is present for classes.

clue.text: Dupes bound for money-lending establishment

blocks.note: pawns are people used and manipulated by others
to hop is to bound, to leap

explanation.surface: Gullible people heading off to borrow money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound for' reads as heading towards, but 'bound' is a verb meaning leap and 'for' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: A pawnbroker's premises lend money against items left as security, so it is a business that makes loans.

clue.text: Concerned with telling on Blair’s principal half?

indicators.note: half of a word means only one of its two halves survives and the rest is cut

blocks.note: relating a story is telling it
Tony is Blair's first name, and only its first two letters are kept

explanation.surface: Someone informing on Blair's other half, his wife Cherie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' is the positional link meaning placed after, and 'Blair's principal' means his first name, Tony, not his chief adviser.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to means about or regarding, the same sense as concerned with in phrases such as 'matters concerned with tax'.

clue.text: Eden: hard going, masculine? The opposite

indicators.note: going means leaving, so this letter departs from the word

blocks.note: Anthony Eden was a British Prime Minister; his first name loses H, for hard
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard, the letter removed
M is the grammar abbreviation for masculine

explanation.surface: A verdict on Prime Minister Anthony Eden: tough and manly, or rather the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Eden was Prime Minister in the 1950s; the clue uses his first name, and 'The opposite' sounds like a closing quip but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An antonym is a word of contrary meaning, such as hot for cold, so it is the opposite of another word.

clue.text: Financial exploiter certain to get City’s protection

indicators.note: getting shelter means being sheltered within something, so one part sits inside another

blocks.note: sure means certain
Ur, the ancient Mesopotamian city, wraps around

explanation.surface: A predatory financier is sure to be shielded by the City of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City' looks like London's financial district, which suits a financier, but it is Ur, a favourite three-letter city in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A usurer lends money at exorbitant interest, preying on borrowers, which makes him someone who exploits people for money.

clue.text: see 28ac.
Cable primarily linked to foolhardy financial disaster

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, pointing to the opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
rash means foolhardy, reckless

explanation.surface: Business Secretary Vince Cable blamed for a reckless economic catastrophe.
explanation.walkthrough: Vince Cable was the Liberal Democrat Business Secretary famous for predicting the 2008 financial collapse.
explanation.definitionFit: A crash is a sudden collapse of markets or prices, as in the 1929 or 2008 stock market crashes.

clue.text: Mounted by a solitary player from United, player who’s knackered

indicators.note: knackered means broken and worn out, so these letters are wrecked into a new order

blocks.note: people who are united act as ONE, and a MAN is a player in a team
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A worn-out footballer from Manchester United being hoisted onto teammates' shoulders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'United' looks like the football club, but it means together as one. 'Knackered' is British slang for exhausted.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-man show is a stage performance staged by a single performer, which is a production put on by one actor.

clue.text: She’s vibrating with inner guard

indicators.note: vibrating things shake about, so these letters are jostled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman using a vibrator, with a bodyguard standing by.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', part of the surface sentence only.
explanation.definitionFit: To enshrine something is to preserve and protect it, as rights are enshrined in law, so it is to guard it.

clue.text: Apple-like launch of computer: “Sexy but not ace”

indicators.note: the launch of anything is its start, so the opening letter is taken
'but not' means except for, so the named letter is left out

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
raunchy means sexy; the A, for ace, is removed
A is the abbreviation for ace on playing cards, the letter removed

explanation.surface: A review of Apple's latest computer launch that calls it sexy but not brilliant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apple-like' points to the tech company, but the definition means like the fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A fresh apple is firm and crisp, making a noise when bitten, so something like an apple in texture is crisp.

clue.text: Lordy, Boris is off – moved by new romantic poet

indicators.note: off means removed, so the preceding small word goes away
things that are moved are shifted about, so their letters change places

blocks.note: taken as written
the name loses its own last two letters, as the clue says
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: An exclamation that Boris Johnson is leaving, displaced by a new romantic.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a reaction to political news; New Romantic was a 1980s pop movement.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Byron was one of the leading English Romantic poets, author of Don Juan and Childe Harold's Pilgrimage.

clue.text: Who’s only turned on when partner is stiff?

definitions.text: Who’s only turned on when partner is stiff?

blocks.clueFragment: Who’s only turned on when partner is stiff?
blocks.note: surface reading: a person aroused only by a partner's erection
setter's reading: a stiff is slang for a corpse, so the partner is dead

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stiff' looks like sexual arousal; in slang a stiff is a dead body, which turns the clue into a description of a sexual attraction to corpses.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a person sexually attracted to dead bodies, whose only partner would be a cadaver with rigor mortis.

clue.text: Abandon inhibition and become a slut?

blocks.note: first meaning: relax and behave freely, without restraint
second meaning: stop taking care of your appearance, slut in its old sense of a slovenly woman

explanation.walkthrough: Slut here has its older British meaning of a slovenly, untidy woman, not a promiscuous one, though the surface wants the latter.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both to relax and act without restraint, and to stop caring about grooming and become slovenly.

clue.text: Balls wants Express or otherwise Telegraph leader

indicators.note: otherwise means in a different way, so these letters are arranged differently
the leader of anything is at the front, so the first letter is taken

blocks.note: to utter is to express in words
taken as written, to be rearranged
the opening letter of the newspaper's name

explanation.surface: Ed Balls, the Labour politician, wanting the Express or Telegraph to back him with an editorial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' looks like Ed Balls, Labour's shadow chancellor, but it is British slang for nonsense. The Express and Telegraph are British newspapers.
explanation.definitionFit: Balls and utter rot are both British slang exclamations meaning complete nonsense, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Flighty thing gives smack if one enters

indicators.note: the answer becomes the longer word when this letter goes in, so the letter is missing from it

blocks.note: smack is slang for heroin
I is the Roman numeral one, the letter missing

explanation.surface: A flirty woman lashes out if anyone comes in.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay runs backwards: the answer plus I gives the drug. 'Flighty' suggests flirtatious but means able to fly.
explanation.definitionFit: A heron is a large wading bird, and birds are creatures that take to the air, which the word 'flighty' playfully captures.

clue.text: In Acapulco, the nod for a bender

blocks.note: el is Spanish for the, and Acapulco is in Mexico
a bow is a nod of the head

explanation.surface: In a Mexican resort, someone agrees to go on a drinking spree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bender' sounds like a drinking binge; it is literally a thing that bends.
explanation.definitionFit: The elbow is the joint where the arm flexes, so it is something that bends.

clue.text: Move clumsily, inserting length twice into Hank

indicators.note: inserting means putting something inside, so one piece goes in the middle of another

blocks.note: a hank is a coil or loop of yarn or rope
L is the abbreviation for length, taken two times

explanation.surface: Instructions for clumsy movement, doubling the length into a skein.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hank' looks like a man's name thanks to the capital, but it is a coil of yarn.
explanation.definitionFit: To lollop is to move in an ungainly, bounding way, like a large dog, so it is to move clumsily.

clue.text: Regulator dubiously soft on Sun chief?

indicators.note: dubiously means in a doubtful, unreliable manner, so these letters are not in their real order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the chief of a newspaper such as the Sun is its editor, ED

explanation.surface: A watchdog accused of going easy on the Sun's editor.
explanation.walkthrough: Ofsted is England's schools inspectorate; 'Sun chief' sounds like Rupert Murdoch but is just an editor.
explanation.definitionFit: Ofsted, the Office for Standards in Education, inspects and regulates schools in England, so it is an official watchdog.

clue.text: Balls could say goodbye to a solid figure in such a freeze?

definitions.text: Balls could say goodbye to a solid figure in such a freeze?

blocks.clueFragment: Balls could say goodbye to a solid figure
blocks.note: surface reading: Ed Balls bidding farewell to a stable statistic in an economic freeze
setter's reading: cold enough to freeze the balls off a metal statue of an ape, the British saying

explanation.walkthrough: The British saying 'cold enough to freeze the balls off a brass monkey' underlies it; 'Balls' looks like Ed Balls and 'solid figure' like a firm statistic.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is informal British slang for extremely cold conditions, after the saying about a metal ape losing its testicles.

clue.text: Futile state to cut back on employment – Tyneside’s first to suffer

indicators.note: first points to the opening letter of the word that follows it

blocks.note: to use less is to cut back on using something
Tyneside is in the North East of England, NE, plus the possessive S
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: The government trims jobs, and the North East around Newcastle is hit first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Employment' reads as jobs, but it means use. Tyneside, around Newcastle, lies in North East England.
explanation.definitionFit: Uselessness is the quality of being without purpose or effect, which is what a futile condition amounts to.

clue.text: Obama needs to ‘internalise’ Republican jeer

indicators.note: to internalise is to take something into oneself, so a piece goes inside

blocks.note: Barack is President Obama's first name
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: President Obama must absorb Republican heckling without reacting.
explanation.walkthrough: To barrack is British and Australian usage for heckling a speaker or team.
explanation.definitionFit: To barrack is to shout scornful remarks at a speaker or player, which is the same as to jeer at them.

clue.text: Virgin bust, a nit to appear before court

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so these letters are smashed and reassembled

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A Virgin Media boss arrested, an idiot summoned to court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' looks like arrested, but it marks the rearrangement; a nit is British for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A virgin is sexually untouched, and intact describes something whole and unbroken, the same sense applied to virginity.

clue.text: Leader’s opportunity to win over the Conference, say, is one sketchy mess full of piss

definitions.text: Leader’s opportunity to win over the Conference, say

indicators.note: a mess is a jumble, so these letters are thrown into confusion and reordered
something full of a substance has it inside, so one piece goes within

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
pee is another word for piss

explanation.surface: A sneer at a party leader's conference address as a sketchy mess, full of hot air and worse.
explanation.walkthrough: The urine word goes among the letters before the whole lot is rearranged. Party leaders give a big speech at the annual British party conference.
explanation.definitionFit: A keynote speech is the main address at a conference, the party leader's chance to rally delegates, of which this is an example.

clue.text: Dim little one gets chlorine on organ

blocks.note: 'un is a dialect form of one, as in 'a little 'un' for a child
Cl is the chemical symbol for chlorine
the ear is an organ of hearing

explanation.surface: A dim-witted toddler gets bleach poured on a body part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dim' looks like a description of the little one, but it is the definition in its sense of indistinct.
explanation.definitionFit: Dim means faint or indistinct, hard to see or make out, and unclear has that same sense of being hazy.

clue.text: Takes on party mired in dodgy past

indicators.note: dodgy means unreliable and suspect, so these letters are not in their true order
something mired is stuck deep inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a do is a party
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A political party with a murky history takes on new members.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' looks political, but it is DO, a celebration.
explanation.definitionFit: To adopt a cause, child or policy is to take it on as one's own responsibility, so adopts and takes on match.

clue.text: Drug-dropping Miley twerking with CBSO representative

indicators.note: dropping something means letting it go, so a letter falls away
twerking is a dance of wild hip-shaking, so these letters are jiggled into a new order

blocks.note: E is ecstasy, the drug removed
the singer's name with E taken away
taken as written; the CBSO is the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra

explanation.surface: Miley Cyrus gives up drugs and twerks with the Birmingham orchestra.
explanation.walkthrough: Miley Cyrus's twerking at the 2013 MTV awards was big news; E for ecstasy is a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Something symbolic stands for something else, which is what representative means in the sense of standing as a sign.

clue.text: ‘Love Bishop’ with sexless suit is a liability

indicators.note: sexless means lacking sex, so the crossword's usual word for sex is taken away

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
litigation is a lawsuit, here losing IT, a coy word for sex

explanation.surface: A clergyman known for romance faces a celibacy lawsuit that becomes a burden.
explanation.walkthrough: IT for sex is a crossword convention, so 'sexless' means remove IT.
explanation.definitionFit: An obligation is a duty or debt one is bound to meet, and a liability is likewise something one owes.

clue.text: On which young hopefuls would be had for a film role

definitions.text: On which young hopefuls would be had for a film role

blocks.clueFragment: On which young hopefuls would be had for a film role
blocks.note: surface reading: a place where aspiring actors are interviewed for a part
setter's reading: 'had' means seduced, the notorious practice of sex in exchange for a part

explanation.walkthrough: 'Had' looks like 'had in for an audition', but it means used sexually, alluding to producers trading parts for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase refers to the sofa in a producer's office where actors were allegedly pressured into sex in exchange for roles.

clue.text: Made more bland, in familiar Blair fashion?

blocks.note: first meaning: softened, made less harsh or striking
second meaning, whimsical: brought down to the style of 'Tone', a familiar name for Tony Blair

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is a joke: Tony Blair's pals might call him 'Tone', so to be 'Toned' is to be made Blair-like, and New Labour was accused of diluting its policies.
explanation.definitionFit: Toned down is the past tense of the phrasal verb meaning to soften or moderate something, making it less vivid or extreme.

clue.text: EU mad with Putin (not one to set the right note)

indicators.note: not means leaving something out, so the letter that follows is removed
mad means crazed and disordered, so these letters lose their sane order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the Russian leader's name without its I
I is the Roman numeral one, the letter removed

explanation.surface: The European Union is furious with Vladimir Putin, who is not the man to strike the right tone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The right note' reads as diplomatic tone, but it is musical pitch; the I comes out of Putin before the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: To tune up is to adjust an instrument so that it plays at the correct pitch, the musical sense of setting notes right.

clue.text: Pissed on top intellectual

blocks.note: high means drunk or intoxicated
the brow is the top of a hill, or the top of the face

explanation.surface: A drunk academic sounding off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pissed' is British slang for drunk, not angry as in American usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Highbrow describes a person or work of refined, scholarly tastes, so it is a synonym for an intellectual.

clue.text: Put away Carter’s nuts in a nice shift

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so these letters go haywire into a new order
to shift is to move about, so these letters change places

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A former president, gone mad, is locked up in a pleasant change of scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put away' tempts as storing something, but it means sent to prison.
explanation.definitionFit: To put someone away is informal for jailing them, and to incarcerate is to imprison or confine.

clue.text: Caption Palin almost used as a candidate’s approach?

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter is cut
used means worked over and handled, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
Sarah Palin's surname without its final letter

explanation.surface: A photo caption of Sarah Palin used to sum up a politician's campaign style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Candidate' looks like an election candidate, given Palin, but it is a job applicant.
explanation.definitionFit: An application is the formal request a job seeker submits, the way a candidate approaches an employer.

clue.text: Political scheming causing revolutions as well as drug-pushing?

blocks.note: wheeling means turning in circles, making revolutions
and means as well as
dealing is selling drugs

explanation.surface: Political plotting that both sparks uprisings and runs a drugs trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutions' looks political, but it means turning circles.
explanation.definitionFit: Wheeling and dealing is the informal idiom for shrewd, often unscrupulous negotiation and manipulation, as in politics or business.

clue.text: Berlusconi’s capital backing soul movement year, Berlusconi-fashion?
